proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an integer \(n\ge3\). The set
\[
\{d\in\mathbb Z:d\ge2,\ d\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty because it contains \(n\), and it is finite because each of its elements lies between \(2\) and \(n\). Hence its minimum \(\ell(n)\) is well defined.

Let \(k\) be a positive divisor of \(n\), and put \(r=n/k\). Then \(r\) is a positive integer. By \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\), the block size \(k\) is eligible at \(R=4\) exactly when
\[
\binom{2n/k}{n/k}=\binom{2r}{r}\ge4,
\]
and its retained focal count is \(2nk\). If \(k=n\), then \(r=1\), and
\[
\binom{2r}{r}=\binom21=2<4,
\]
so \(k=n\) is ineligible.

Suppose instead that \(k\) is a proper divisor of \(n\). Because \(k\) and \(n\) are positive and \(k<n\), the integer \(r=n/k\) satisfies \(r\ge2\). Direct calculation gives
\[
\binom42=6.
\]
Moreover, for every positive integer \(s\), positivity of the factorials permits division and yields
\[
\frac{\binom{2(s+1)}{s+1}}{\binom{2s}{s}}
=\frac{(2s+2)(2s+1)}{(s+1)^2}
=\frac{2(2s+1)}{s+1}>1,
\]
where the last inequality follows from \(2(2s+1)-(s+1)=3s+1>0\). Induction from \(s=2\) therefore gives
\[
\binom{2r}{r}\ge\binom42=6\ge4.
\]
Thus every proper divisor \(k\mid n\) is eligible. We have proved that the eligible block sizes at \(R=4\) are exactly the proper positive divisors of \(n\).

The score \(2nk\) is strictly increasing in \(k\) because \(2n>0\). For a proper divisor \(k\), the co-divisor \(d=n/k\) is a divisor of \(n\) satisfying \(d\ge2\), and conversely every such \(d\) gives the proper divisor \(k=n/d\). Since division of the positive number \(n\) is order reversing on positive denominators, the largest eligible \(k\) corresponds to the smallest such \(d\), namely \(d=\ell(n)\). Hence \(\textnormal{def:equal-square-comparator}\) gives the exact published-subclass optimum
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2n\frac{n}{\ell(n)}
=\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
In particular this quantity is positive, so every later division by it is valid.

The hypotheses of the already established \(\textnormal{prop:r4-reduction}\) hold because \(n_B=n_S=n\ge3\). That proposition gives the exact covering paired-rectangle frontier
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
Subtracting the preceding exact comparator formula proves
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}.
\]
Likewise, positivity of \(2n^2/\ell(n)\) permits division, and elementary algebra gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
&=\frac{2(n-1)^2+2}{2n^2/\ell(n)}\\
&=\ell(n)\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}\\
&=\ell(n)\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

By definition \(\ell(n)\ge2\), so
\[
\frac{2n^2}{\ell(n)}\le n^2.
\]
Substitution in the exact gap gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
&\ge2(n-1)^2+2-n^2\\
&=(n-2)^2>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where strict positivity uses \(n\ge3\). The factor
\[
1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}=\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n^2}
\]
is positive. Multiplying \(\ell(n)\ge2\) by this factor therefore gives
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in either lower bound holds exactly when \(2n^2/\ell(n)=n^2\), equivalently when \(\ell(n)=2\). By the definition of \(\ell(n)\), the equality \(\ell(n)=2\) holds exactly when \(2\mid n\), that is, exactly when \(n\) is even.

The ratio lower bound converges to \(2\) as \(n\to\infty\), hence
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}\ge2.
\]
For every even \(n\), the equality case just proved gives
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}\longrightarrow2
\]
along the infinite sequence of even integers. The full limit inferior is therefore at most \(2\), and the two inequalities prove that it equals \(2\).

Finally, if \(n\) is prime, its only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(n\), so \(\ell(n)=n\). Substitution into the exact formulas yields
\[
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n,
\]
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
=2(n-1)^2+2-2n
=2(n-1)(n-2),
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
=n\left(1-\frac2n+\frac{2}{n^2}\right)
=n-2+\frac2n.
\]
This is the claimed prime-size linear-scale ratio separation.

proposed.justification: The exact least-divisor formula shows that the catalog is not merely a notational enlargement of the published equal-square family: unequal covering rectangles strictly improve focal retention for every balanced size \(n\ge3\), even sizes give the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and prime sizes give ratio \(n-2+2/n\).
proposed.gap: The published equal-square calculation optimizes only over equal block sizes and does not identify that its support-four optimum is \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), nor the resulting exact separation from the covering paired-rectangle frontier.
proposed.consumer: Researchers using the published equal-block rule can compute its exact support-four benchmark from the least nontrivial divisor of the balanced population size and quantify the precise focal-size gain from allowing unequal covering rectangles.

prose_updates.tldr: For independently and uniformly half-randomized populations on two unequal market sides, the optimal covering rectangle at required support \(R\) reduces to a finite residual catalog depending only on \(R\). For \(R\ge4\) and \(n_B,n_S\ge4R\), the exact frontier is the maximum of finitely many affine catalog scores and every tie is retained. On balanced squares at \(R=4\), if \(\ell(n)\) is the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, then the published equal-square optimum is exactly \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), while the covering paired-rectangle optimum is \(2(n-1)^2+2\). Their exact ratio is \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\): even sizes form the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, whereas prime sizes have ratio \(n-2+2/n\). A constant-incidence sampler implements the selected event, and null-adjusted focal outcomes yield exact one-sided inversion for a sharp constant total effect. No universal collapse of the catalog to diagonal unit residuals is claimed.

project_justification.gap: The closest exact two-sided-market method proves validity for selected equal blocks and treats block choice within that published equal-square subclass; it neither identifies the support-four optimum \(2n^2/\ell(n)\) from the least nontrivial divisor nor optimizes over unequal covering rectangles. General biclique methods establish validity and power guidance but do not classify the optimal covering paired rectangle. Marketplace bias-and-variance analyses motivate the design problem but do not solve this exact rectangle optimization, and existing one-dimensional subset-sum purification does not preserve a prescribed common buyer--seller target fiber.
project_justification.niche: Balanced independent randomization converts admissible covering rectangles into two coupled half-sum profiles. This structure permits an exact finite residual reduction and affine phase analysis for unequal market-side sizes. On the balanced \(R=4\) slice it also yields an exact arithmetic classification of the published equal-square benchmark through \(\ell(n)\), the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, without asserting an unrestricted-biclique optimum.
project_justification.fill: A two-stage concentration argument bounds the residual on the smaller side and uses a support-preserving residual-copy comparison to bound the larger residual. This yields a finite catalog and an exact affine frontier with all catalog ties. At \(R=4\), every proper equal-block divisor is eligible, so the published equal-square optimum is exactly \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), versus the covering paired-rectangle value \(2(n-1)^2+2\). The exact ratio \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\) has its sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope on even sizes and equals \(n-2+2/n\) at prime sizes. The same catalog supports an implementable conditional law and exact one-sided sharp-null inversion. Whether every catalog entry can be purified to a dominating diagonal unit-residual entry remains a separate open question.

prose_updates.related_work: Liu, Shaikh, and Toulis (2026) establish the equal \(k\)-block total-effect test and motivate the support--focal-size trade-off. Within their published equal-square subclass, the present result proves that the exact support-four optimum is \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=2n^2/\ell(n)\), with \(\ell(n)\) the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, and compares it with the exact covering paired-rectangle optimum \(2(n-1)^2+2\). Even sizes give the sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, while prime sizes give ratio \(n-2+2/n\). Puelz, Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2022) encode imputable tests as bicliques and motivate large bicliques, but do not supply the paired-rectangle classification. Li, Zhao, Johari, and Weintraub (2021) study interference-induced bias and variance in two-sided marketplace experiments, and Johari, Li, Liskovich, and Weintraub (2022) analyze bias under two-sided platform designs; both motivate why focal retention and design choice matter, but neither is a competing exact covering-rectangle optimization result. Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2019) provide the conditioning-mechanism validity theorem used after imputability is verified. Basse, Ding, Feller, and Toulis (2024) provide the orbit-equivariance template, while unequal rectangular profiles require a separate constant-incidence count. Luo, Dasgupta, Xie, and Liu (2021) provide discrete Fisher inversion machinery, specialized here after null-adjusted dyadic imputability and crossing monotonicity are established. Singhal (2019) motivates bilinear subset-sum profiles and one-dimensional purification, but does not furnish a coupled common-fiber-preserving reduction to diagonal unit residuals. Ye et al. (2023) provide the unequal-side marketplace consumer through Platform O's independent user-view and ad randomizations.
prose_updates.interpretation: The finite-catalog result is the actionable design certificate: for fixed resolution \(R\), one enumerates \(\mathcal C_R\), evaluates the affine scores at the two market sizes, and retains every maximizer on a phase boundary. The balanced-square \(R=4\) slice has a complete arithmetic comparator: letting \(\ell(n)\) be the least divisor of \(n\) at least two, the best published equal-square profile retains \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), while the optimal covering paired rectangle retains \(2(n-1)^2+2\). The exact ratio is \(\ell(n)(1-2/n+2/n^2)\). Even sizes, for which \(\ell(n)=2\), attain the sharp lower envelope \(2-4/n+4/n^2\) and establish limit inferior two; prime sizes, for which \(\ell(n)=n\), have ratio \(n-2+2/n\) and therefore a linear-scale separation. These comparisons concern the published equal-square subclass, not unrestricted bicliques. The unresolved unit-residual question concerns only whether the already finite computation admits a further universal closed-form collapse; it is not needed for catalog optimality, this exact comparison, sampling, or exact one-sided inversion.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The note proves the finite residual catalog, exact affine frontier and catalog equality cases, the constant-incidence sampler, and exact one-sided inversion under the sharp constant total-effect null. On balanced squares at \(R=4\), it also proves the exact published equal-square comparator formula \(2n^2/\ell(n)\), the exact gap and ratio against the covering paired-rectangle optimum, the sharp even-size factor-two asymptotic lower envelope, and the prime-size ratio \(n-2+2/n\). Universal unit-residual purification remains an explicit unresolved question and is not used by those results. The note makes no claim about weak-null validity, power or confidence-width optimality, unrestricted bicliques, minimality of the \(4R\) threshold, ordinary two-sided \(95\)-percent inversion at support \(20\), or the empirical validity of the constant-effect exposure model for Platform O.
